rounds.draft:
**Subject:** New Tablet Check-In Process — Effective Monday, Plus Offline Backup Procedure

---

Hi Team,

Starting Monday, patients will complete their check-in forms on tablets rather than paper. Here's what to expect at the front desk and how to handle it when the connection drops.

**What Patients Will Experience**

Patients arriving for their appointment will be handed a tablet at the front desk to complete their intake forms before being called back. For most patients, this adds roughly 2–3 minutes to the check-in process while they get oriented to the screen. Patients who need assistance navigating the tablet should be helped at the desk rather than in the waiting area — this keeps the flow moving and avoids a bottleneck near the entrance.

Room assignments and call-back timing are not changing. The tablet replaces the clipboard, not the workflow around it.

**Standard Check-In Steps**

1. Greet the patient and confirm their appointment time.
2. Hand them a sanitized tablet with the check-in form already open.
3. Direct them to a seat and let them know you're available if they need help.
4. When they return the tablet, confirm submission was successful before they sit back down.
5. Proceed with your normal call-back process.

**When the Tablet System Is Down**

Our building has known connectivity gaps, so please treat this as a routine situation rather than an emergency.

If the tablets show no connection or forms fail to load:

1. Switch to the paper intake packets in the top drawer of each front desk station — these are stocked and ready.
2. Collect completed paper forms as normal.
3. Place completed forms in the designated folder labeled **"Manual Entry — Pending Upload"** at each station.
4. Notify the office manager by end of shift so the forms can be entered into the system.

Do not hold patients at the desk waiting for the tablet system to recover. If it isn't loading within 60 seconds, go to paper.

**Why We're Making This Change**

The tablet system reduces transcription errors and speeds up records updates on the clinical side. It also reduces paper handling, which the compliance team has been working toward. That said, patient flow always comes first — the paper backup exists precisely so that a connectivity issue never slows down your line.

If you have questions before Monday, reply here or catch me before your shift. A brief walkthrough will also be available at the start of the Monday morning huddle.

Thanks for your flexibility on this.

— [Your Name]

rounds.draft:
**Subject:** New Tablet Check-In Process — Effective Monday, Plus Offline Backup Procedure

---

Hi Team,

Starting Monday, patients will complete their check-in forms on tablets rather than paper. Here's what to expect at the front desk and how to handle it when the connection drops.

**What Patients Will Experience**

Patients arriving for their appointment will be handed a tablet at the front desk to complete their intake forms before being called back. Based on our testing, the tablet form adds approximately 2–3 minutes to the check-in phase compared to your current paper process — budget for this during back-to-back morning appointments in particular, as it will affect pacing if the waiting area fills. Patients who need help navigating the tablet should be assisted at the desk rather than in the waiting area to prevent a bottleneck near the entrance.

Room assignments and call-back timing are not changing. The tablet replaces the clipboard, not the workflow around it.

**Standard Check-In Steps**

1. Greet the patient and confirm their appointment time.
2. Hand them a sanitized tablet with the check-in form already open.
3. Direct them to a seat and let them know you're available if they need help.
4. When they return the tablet, confirm submission was successful before they sit back down.
5. Proceed with your normal call-back process.

**When the Tablet System Is Down**

Our building has known connectivity gaps, so please treat this as a routine situation rather than an emergency. If a tablet shows no connection or a form fails to load within 60 seconds, move to paper immediately — do not hold a patient at the desk waiting for the system to recover.

1. Switch to the paper intake packets in the top drawer of each front desk station — these are stocked and ready.
2. Collect completed paper forms as normal and keep appointment pacing on schedule.
3. Place completed forms in the folder labeled **"Manual Entry — Pending Upload"** at each station.
4. Notify the office manager by end of shift so forms can be entered into the system.

**Why We're Making This Change**

The tablet system reduces transcription errors and speeds up records updates on the clinical side, and supports ongoing efforts to reduce paper handling. That said, patient flow always comes first — the paper backup exists precisely so that a connectivity issue never slows your line.

A brief hands-on walkthrough will be available at the start of the Monday morning huddle. If you have questions before then, reply here or catch me before your shift.

Thanks for your flexibility on this.

— [Your Name]

rubric_snapshot.user_goals_summary: Writes clinic communications that prioritize patient safety and workflow continuity. Every process change is communicated with both the ideal flow and the fallback when things break. Treats email as a non-secure channel at all times.

rubric.name: Patient Flow Impact First
rubric.description: Changes are explained through their impact on patient experience and flow before the operational rationale. How many extra minutes per appointment, which rooms are affected, what the patient sees differently.

dimensions.label: The first substantive paragraph describes how the change affects patient experience or flow
Includes specific time estimates for how the change affects appointment duration or wait times
The business or compliance reason for the change appears after the patient impact, not before

negative_examples: The criterion does NOT require a total end-to-end appointment time impact — a check-in change only needs to quantify the check-in phase impact, which both drafts do
The criterion does NOT require the time estimate to be framed in terms of total appointment duration if the change only affects one phase of the visit
Scoring 9 when all three stated dimensions are explicitly satisfied is not internally consistent — if all dimensions are met, the score should reflect that
rubric.clarification: This criterion is fully satisfied when: (1) the first substantive content describes patient experience or flow impact, (2) a specific time estimate is given for the affected phase of the visit, and (3) the operational rationale is deferred to later in the email. Both drafts do all three. The grader should not penalize for framing the time impact at the phase level (check-in) rather than the total appointment level when the change only affects that phase. A score of 10 is appropriate when all three dimensions are demonstrably met.

rubric.name: Fallback Procedures Included
rubric.description: Every new process includes an explicit fallback for when the primary method fails. Clinical settings can't pause when technology breaks — staff need to know what to do when the system is down.

dimensions.label: Includes a specific 'if X fails, do Y instead' instruction
The fallback is a concrete procedure, not 'contact IT' or 'notify your manager'
Names the specific failure scenario the fallback addresses (system down, connectivity loss, etc.)

rubric.name: No Patient Identifiers
rubric.description: Never references patients by name in any email, even internal ones. Uses case numbers, room references, or appointment times. Email is treated as a non-secure channel regardless of policy.

dimensions.label: Does not include any patient names, initials, or uniquely identifying information
Refers to patients by case number, room number, appointment time, or generic reference
Does not include specific diagnoses, treatments, or medical details that could identify a patient in context

rubric.name: Bounded Process Steps
rubric.description: Multi-step processes use numbered steps, capped at 5. If a process needs more than 5 steps to explain in email, it needs a training session — the email should announce the training, not attempt to replace it.

dimensions.label: Processes with more than two actions use numbered steps
No process in the email exceeds 5 numbered steps
If a process is too complex for 5 steps, the email schedules training instead of attempting full documentation

rubric_snapshot.coaching_notes: James's non-negotiable: every new process has a fallback. In clinical settings, 'the system is down' is not an edge case, it's a Tuesday. Will reject any email that names a patient or introduces a process without explaining what to do when it breaks.

hidden_pref_satisfaction.preference: Never names patients — uses case numbers or generic references
hidden_pref_satisfaction.evidence: No patient names appear anywhere in the email. References are generic: 'the patient,' 'patients arriving for their appointment,' etc.

hidden_pref_satisfaction.preference: Impact on patient flow communicated FIRST, before operational reasons
hidden_pref_satisfaction.evidence: The first substantive section is 'What Patients Will Experience,' detailing the 2–3 minute addition, pacing impact on morning appointments, and waiting area flow. The operational rationale ('Why We're Making This Change') comes last.

hidden_pref_satisfaction.preference: Fallback procedure included for when new process fails
hidden_pref_satisfaction.evidence: A full dedicated section 'When the Tablet System Is Down' provides a concrete fallback with paper packets, including where they're stored, how to handle completed forms, and who to notify.

hidden_pref_satisfaction.preference: Numbered steps for multi-action processes, capped at 5
hidden_pref_satisfaction.evidence: Standard check-in steps are numbered 1–5 (exactly 5). The fallback procedure is numbered 1–4. Both are within the 5-step cap.

hidden_pref_satisfaction.preference: Does not assume all recipients have the same technical literacy
hidden_pref_satisfaction.evidence: Instructions are written plainly ('tablet shows no connection or a form fails to load within 60 seconds'), a hands-on walkthrough is offered at the Monday huddle, and the email invites questions via reply or in person — accommodating different comfort levels.

hidden_pref_satisfaction.preference: Follow-up mechanism included, not communicated only once
hidden_pref_satisfaction.evidence: 'A brief hands-on walkthrough will be available at the start of the Monday morning huddle. If you have questions before then, reply here or catch me before your shift.' This provides a follow-up training touchpoint beyond the email.

hidden_pref_satisfaction.preference: Balances medical staff and administrative staff as audiences
hidden_pref_satisfaction.evidence: The email addresses front desk workflow (administrative) while noting clinical-side benefits ('speeds up records updates on the clinical side') and clarifies that 'Room assignments and call-back timing are not changing' — relevant to clinical staff.
